Since then, I've been the second choice for several more men. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend (although, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway). Each time, I laughed one of those sad, desperate guffaws -- here we go again! What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me? Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I'm so aware of my "magic touch" that I'm making it happen. While the first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him what may happen. At the time, though, he waved the thought away. "I'm so picky, I rarely really like a girl like I like you," he typed. A month later, he must've been pleasantly shocked to discover my unfortunate power reached across the Atlantic Ocean. When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was angry I'd let this happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it's irrational to use my past experience to predict the outcome of my future relationships (or my attempts at them). I'm sure that there'll be a guy someday who doesn't find me easy to move on from, but in the meantime I can't ignore the pattern and pretend that each time was a coincidence, as Ken had wanted me to do. I don't know if there is a way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Each time I let my hopes conquer my superstition, there's a crash, a burn, a deflation, and the temporary loss of the ability to giggle, but I choose the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the chance for breaking my streak. # The Curse of Being the Girl Before the Girlfriend

*(The Frisky)* -- There exists a school of thought suggesting that if you brace yourself for catastrophe, it won't come to pass. What if my family died in a car accident? What if my house burned down? Two summers ago, I found myself asking a different kind of question: Wouldn't it be devastating if my first love found someone new and moved on before I'd even begun to heal? Thankfully, my family and my house remain unscathed—but my heart, my love life, and my ego are still very much in need of repair.

*What is it about me that propels men into the arms of their dream girls, right after they've been with me?*

"I met someone." The text message lit up my phone screen, and I stopped walking mid-stride. I was leaving the movie theater with a group of friends, and in that instant, it felt as though every feeling he'd ever had for me had been erased in a single night. We'd broken up because he was studying abroad in Europe. With almost cruel irony, we had confessed our feelings for each other just two nights before he left. And then, he became someone else's boyfriend—a relationship that would go on to outlast the one we'd shared.

I should have seen it coming. This wasn't the first time.

My first kiss, who never agreed to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I was still aching over him. They remain together to this day. Since then, I've played runner-up more times than I care to count. The most recent instances came this past summer: I tried, and failed, to win the heart of my friend Ken, who chose to pursue the person he truly wanted rather than settle for me. Then I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend—though, in fairness, I suspect they were meant to end up together regardless.

Each time, I let out that particular kind of laugh—equal parts sad and desperate—the one that says, *here we go again.* What is it about me that sends men straight into the arms of their dream girls the moment we part ways?

Perhaps there's a more fitting explanation than superstition: the self-fulfilling prophecy. Maybe I'm so convinced of my "magic touch" that I'm unwittingly conjuring it into existence. When my first love left for Europe, I even warned him what might happen. He brushed it off at the time. "I'm picky," he told me. "I rarely like a girl the way I like you." A month later, he must have been genuinely surprised to discover that my curse had followed him across the Atlantic.

When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was furious—furious that I'd let this happen to me yet again. I lashed out at him, and he countered that it was irrational to let past experiences dictate the outcome of future relationships, or my attempts at them. I'd like to believe that someday, I'll meet a man who doesn't find me so easy to move on from. But for now, I can't simply dismiss the pattern as coincidence, however much Ken might wish I would.

I don't know if there's any way to outrun what feels inevitable. Every time I let hope override my superstition, it ends the same way: a crash, a burn, a quiet deflation, and a temporary loss of my ability to laugh at any of it. And yet, I'd still rather take my chances at being the girl before the girlfriend than give up entirely on the possibility of breaking the streak.

I'm not certain there's any way to escape what feels like an unavoidable fate. Yet I'd still rather risk being the girl who came before the girlfriend than pass up any chance to finally break this cycle.

# The Pattern I Can't Seem to Escape

There's a peculiar phenomenon I've noticed throughout my romantic history, one that has followed me with an almost eerie consistency: the men I develop genuine feelings for seem to find "the girl of their dreams" shortly after whatever connection we shared comes to an end. It's as if my presence in their lives serves as some kind of catalyst—clearing the path, perhaps, for them to recognize what they're truly looking for, just not with me.

The pattern first emerged with my first love. We parted ways when he left to study in Europe, a separation that felt devastating at the time but seemed, in retrospect, almost inevitable given the circumstances. What stung more than the breakup itself was what followed: shortly after our split, he entered into a relationship that would last for years. I watched from a distance as he built the kind of lasting partnership I had hoped we might create together.

I told myself this was a fluke, a one-time coincidence born of circumstance and distance. But then it happened again with my first kiss. He was someone I had genuine hope for, someone I wanted to call my boyfriend, but he declined to take that step with me. I held onto feelings for him long after that rejection, watching with a complicated mixture of hurt and something like resignation as he eventually found lasting love with another woman entirely. Once again, I was left wondering what it was about me that seemed to precede—perhaps even facilitate—someone else's happiness with the person I had wanted for myself.

If two instances felt like coincidence, the pattern's continuation into my more recent experiences has made me question whether something deeper is at play. There was Ken, who made it clear he was pursuing someone he genuinely wanted, someone who wasn't me. And then there was Brian, whose story took an even more pointed turn: he reunited with his ex-girlfriend, choosing to return to a past relationship rather than explore whatever possibility existed between us.

Now, having watched this scenario play out repeatedly across different men, different circumstances, and different points in my life, I find myself grappling with an uncomfortable question: Have I somehow created a self-fulfilling prophecy? Is it possible that my growing awareness of this "magic touch"—this uncanny ability to precede someone else's romantic fulfillment—has become so ingrained in my psyche that I'm unconsciously enacting it? Perhaps my heightened consciousness of the pattern has made me anxious or self-sabotaging in ways I don't fully recognize, subtly pushing away the very connections I'm hoping to nurture. Or perhaps I'm simply pattern-matching coincidences into something more meaningful than they actually are, my mind seeking narrative and causation where none truly exists.

Either way, the question lingers: am I the common denominator creating my own outcome, or merely a bystander to an unfortunate string of romantic timing that has nothing to do with me at all?

# The Magic Touch

I have a theory about myself, one I've tested against the evidence of my own heart more times than I'd like to admit. I call it my "magic touch," though there's nothing magical about it in the traditional sense—unless you count the particular alchemy of watching men transform into devoted partners approximately three to six months after they've stopped wanting to be with me.

It started, as these patterns often do, with something I dismissed as bad luck. There was Daniel, who I dated for four months in my mid-twenties, who told me he "wasn't ready for anything serious" right before he got serious with someone else exactly seven weeks later. I remember scrolling through his engagement photos eighteen months after that, doing the mental math, trying to figure out where I fit into the timeline of his becoming ready.

Then there was the pattern repeating with Marcus, with Sam, with the barista I went on three dates with before he mentioned—almost as an aside—that he'd started seeing someone from his gym. Six months later: moved in together. A year after that: an engagement post with a caption about "finally finding my person."

Finally finding. As if I had been some kind of practice round, a rough draft before the real manuscript.

At first, I told myself this was simply confirmation bias—that I was only noticing the cases that fit my narrative while conveniently forgetting the men who dated other women after me and then broke up with them just as quickly, or never found anyone at all. Surely, I reasoned, this was just the ordinary chaos of dating, the law of large numbers playing out in a world where everyone is constantly cycling through connections, and I was simply pattern-matching my way into a narrative of tragedy because tragedy feels more meaningful than randomness.

But the pattern persisted with a consistency that started to feel less like coincidence and more like fate—or, worse, mechanism. I began to wonder if there was something almost superstitious happening, some unconscious act I was performing on the men I loved, in the same way ancient sailors believed certain sailors were cursed to bring storms. Was I the storm? Was my touch bringing something into being, some catalytic transformation, whereby a man became ready for commitment precisely because of the incompatibility he'd discovered with me, or perhaps despite it—maybe it was something in the negative space of our relationship that clarified for him what he wanted, the way a photograph's absence of light defines its subject?

I started to dread new relationships not because I feared heartbreak in the traditional sense, but because I feared this specific, recursive heartbreak: not just losing someone, but losing someone into the arms of a happiness I had somehow made possible for them. Every new connection became tinged with a prophetic dread. I would feel myself falling for someone and simultaneously begin mourning the future girlfriend he hadn't met yet, the one who would benefit from whatever indefinable growth he was clearly on the verge of, growth I could sense but somehow couldn't inspire him toward myself.

And this is where I've started to interrogate my own theory, because I've begun to suspect that my awareness of the pattern is itself part of what perpetuates it.

Here's what I mean: when I go into a new relationship already anticipating its expiration, already scanning for signs that this will be another rehearsal before someone else's real thing, I bring a particular energy to it—a guardedness, perhaps, or an eagerness to perform ease so as not to seem like the anxious woman I'm afraid of becoming. I hold back the version of myself that might actually deepen the connection, because some part of me is already protecting against the loss I've come to expect. I ask fewer real questions. I accept vague answers about the future more readily than I should, because pressing for clarity feels like tempting the very fate I'm trying to avoid.

In other words: maybe I'm not cursed. Maybe I'm cautious in exactly the ways that make my fears self-fulfilling.

If I go into every relationship already grieving its end, if I already see myself as the placeholder rather than the destination, doesn't that certainty communicate itself somehow, in the subtle currency of body language and reduced vulnerability that partners pick up on, even if they can't articulate it? Maybe men sense my own doubt in myself, my own sense that I am simply a way station, and that sensing shapes how they hold the relationship, how much they invest, how easily they let go.

This doesn't fully explain the pattern, of course—it doesn't account for genuine incompatibilities, timing that has nothing to do with me, the simple truth that not everyone is meant to be with everyone else. But it does suggest something uncomfortable: that my "magic touch" might not be a supernatural force acting upon me, but rather an unconscious framework I've built and then unknowingly enacted—a prophecy so anticipated that I ensure its arrival, if only by expecting it too thoroughly to resist it.

Perhaps the real magic isn't in what I do to these men, but in what my expectation does to me: how it shapes the person I become in relationships, how it limits the future I allow myself to imagine within them. If that's true, then the antidote isn't to stop caring about the pattern, but to stop performing my role in it—to enter into connection without already writing the epilogue, without casting myself, before the story has even properly begun, as the character who exits before the happy ending.

I don't know if I can break the spell. But I'm beginning to understand that I might be the one who cast it.

# A Frisky Morning

The sun had barely risen when the puppy began its daily ritual of chaos. There, in the middle of the living room, sat a pile of shredded newspaper—evidence of a job well done, at least in the dog's mind.

The frisky little creature bounded from room to room, tail wagging with an energy that seemed impossible for such an early hour. There was no couch cushion safe from her enthusiasm, no shoe left unclaimed as a chew toy.

"There you are," her owner said with a sigh, spotting her hiding behind the curtains. The dog's ears perked up immediately, sensing a game was about to begin.

There's something infectious about that kind of energy—the pure, unfiltered joy of a creature who hasn't yet learned to contain her excitement. The morning chaos, frustrating as it was, brought a smile to her owner's face.

There would be time later for training, for teaching boundaries and patience. But for now, in this frisky, ridiculous moment, there was only the simple pleasure of watching a young dog discover the world with reckless abandon. The day had just begun, and already it was full of life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal essay for The Frisky about always being "the girl before the girlfriend" in past relationships.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Understudy

I've spent most of my adult life in the wings, watching someone else take the role I rehearsed for months, sometimes years.

There's a particular flavor of heartbreak that doesn't get talked about enough: the ache of being the girl who came *before*. Not the one who got left for someone else, not the one who did the leaving—just the one who did the work. The one who softened him up, who taught him how to communicate, who patiently explained that flowers on a random Tuesday mean more than flowers after a fight. And then, having absorbed all that labor, he'd go on to build something beautiful with someone else.

I used to think I had bad luck. Now I think I had a bad habit.

There was Daniel, who I dated for two years in my mid-twenties. He came to me anxious and avoidant, flinching at the word "relationship" like it was a trap door. I never pushed. I let him set the pace, celebrated his small steps toward vulnerability like they were Olympic feats. By the time we broke up—amicably, exhaustedly—he was a man capable of real intimacy. He married someone eighteen months later. At the wedding, which I was invited to because we'd stayed "friends," his wife gave a speech about how safe he made her feel. I clapped. I meant it. I also went home and cried into a bag of pretzels.

There was Marcus, who I helped through his father's death, who I sat with in emergency rooms, who I taught—patiently, like a kindergarten teacher—how to apologize without getting defensive. His current girlfriend gets the apologies. I got the tantrums.

For a long time, I framed this as a personal tragedy, a cosmic joke at my expense. I was Whitney Houston in "I Will Always Love You," except nobody wrote a song about my specific pain: the pain of being *useful* rather than *chosen*.

But somewhere around my thirtieth birthday, sitting alone in my apartment doing the math on how many years I'd spent as unpaid emotional labor, I started asking harder questions. Why did I keep choosing men who needed fixing? Why did I mistake being needed for being loved? Why was I so drawn to potential instead of the actual present-tense person in front of me?

The answer, uncomfortable as it is, wasn't about them. It was about me.

I liked being necessary. I liked being the missing piece, the answer key, the girl with all the patience in the world. It made me feel powerful in a relationship dynamic where I otherwise felt like I was auditioning for a part I might not get. If I could make myself indispensable, surely he wouldn't leave. Except they did leave—just later than I expected, once the renovation was complete and someone else got to enjoy the finished house.

I don't think these men were villains. I think they were, like most of us, just people trying to become better versions of themselves, and I happened to be a chapter in that story rather than the ending. That's not nothing. But it's also not enough to build a life on.

These days, I'm trying something radical: dating men who are already, more or less, okay. Men who don't need me to excavate them from years of bad patterns. It's strange—almost boring, in the best way. There's less drama, less of that intoxicating sense of *saving* someone. There's also, for the first time, the novel experience of being chosen for who I am rather than what I can build.

I still think about those men sometimes, the ones whose girlfriends benefit from my invisible labor like tenants living in a house I renovated and never got to call home. I hope they're happy. I hope, selfishly, that somewhere they remember me not as a stepping stone but as someone who mattered.

But mostly, I'm trying to stop being the girl before the girlfriend, and start being the girlfriend. It turns out that requires believing I deserve the ending, not just the rough draft. Some days I believe it more than others. But I'm rehearsing—for myself, this time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create a first-person confessional article exploring the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy in dating, using a narrator who keeps losing guys to their eventual girlfriends?
counterfactuals.output:
# I Was Always the Almost

I have a type, and that type is: leaves.

Not leaves as in foliage. Leaves as in *leaves me*. Specifically, leaves me for the woman he marries. I am, professionally speaking, a placeholder. A rough draft. The relationship equivalent of a practice interview you do before the one that actually matters.

This isn't a metaphor. This is a pattern I can chart across a decade with the precision of a woman who has had a lot of time alone to think about it.

There was Kevin, who I dated for eight months in my mid-twenties, who told me he "wasn't ready for anything serious," and who got engaged fourteen months later to a woman he met at a wedding. There was Theo, who ghosted me after four months of what I genuinely thought was something, and who I now follow on Instagram against my own advice, watching him build a life with someone named Priya that involves a rescue dog and a shared Peloton account. There was Marcus. There was David. There is, currently, the looming shadow of a guy named Jonas who I am trying very hard not to think about in these terms, and failing.

For years I told this story as a story about them. Bad luck. Bad timing. Men who weren't ready until, mysteriously, they were ready for someone else.

But I've started to wonder if I've been the common denominator wearing a disguise.

---

Here's the thing about being the almost: you start rehearsing for it. Somewhere in the middle of dating Kevin, I stopped fighting for the relationship and started **preparing for its autopsy**. I remember thinking, *this is the part of the story where it doesn't work out*, while it was still working out. I remember softening my expectations before he'd given me any reason to. I remember, God help me, being almost relieved when it ended, because at least the waiting was over.

That's not intuition. That's a self-fulfilling prophecy wearing intuition's coat.

A psychologist would probably tell you that if you expect to be left, you leave first emotionally, and the guy just catches up to the paperwork. You withhold the version of yourself that might actually be irreplaceable, because some protective, wounded part of you has already decided the ending, and why would you show someone your whole hand in a game you've privately already lost?

I did this. I know I did this, because I can see the difference now in how I talk about Jonas versus how I talked about Kevin. With Kevin, I was careful. Curated. A little bit performing the role of Easygoing Girlfriend, because I didn't trust that the real, needier, more specific version of me could hold his interest. I was already halfway out the door emotionally, just to avoid the indignity of being pushed.

---

The cruelest part of this pattern isn't the breakups. It's the epilogues.

You will, if you are unlucky and terminally online like me, see the *after*. You will see Kevin's fiancée and she will be lovely, and worse than that, she will be recognizably *more herself* in the photos than I ever let myself be in the relationship. She's laughing with her mouth open. She's got opinions in the captions. She looks like a woman who was never rehearsing for her own abandonment.

And I used to think: what does she have that I didn't?

Now I think the more useful question is: what did she *do* that I didn't, which is — nothing performative. She just showed up as the actual, unguarded, occasionally difficult version of herself, presumably because nobody had yet taught her that doing so was dangerous.

I was taught. Every almost taught me a little more. By the time I got to Theo, I was so good at protecting myself from the ending that I'd basically already left the relationship in my head by month two. I called it self-preservation. It was actually self-sabotage with better PR.

---

I don't think this means the guys were blameless — some of them were genuinely just not that into me, and no amount of authentic self-expression was going to override that. I'm not trying to therapize my way into "actually it was always my fault," because that's its own trap, its own way of making yourself the main character of someone else's mediocre decision-making.

But I am trying to sit with the more uncomfortable possibility: that I got so used to being the almost that I started auditioning for the role instead of trying to get cast in a different one entirely.

With Jonas, I've caught myself doing it again — the pre-grieving, the emotional hedging, the careful modulation of how much I text back so that if this ends, I'll have technically protected something. And for the first time, I noticed it happening in real time instead of years later in some essay about my own patterns.

I don't know if noticing is enough to break it. I don't know if I'll look up in eighteen months and find Jonas's future girlfriend laughing with her mouth open in some Instagram caption while I nod along, unsurprised, having already written this ending in my head months ago.

But I'm trying, for once, to close my mouth on the autopsy and just be in the body of the thing while it's still alive.

Worst case, I get another essay out of it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# I Should Be a Dating App, Not a Person

Let's talk about my superpower. No, I can't fly. I can't read minds (though I've gotten scary good at deciphering "we should hang out sometime" as "I have already mentally moved on"). My power is much more insidious: I date a man for a respectable amount of time, we part ways, and within six months he's engaged to someone named Madison who does Pilates and owns a golden retriever named Biscuit.

I am, apparently, a relationship crockpot. You put a man in me, let him simmer, and he comes out perfectly seasoned for someone else to enjoy.

## The Origin Story

It started with my college boyfriend, Kyle. We dated for two years—two *years*, people, that's basically a common-law marriage in your twenties. We broke up because he "wasn't ready to settle down." Reader, eight months later he was down on one knee at a Cheesecake Factory (her choice, apparently, which honestly should have been a bigger red flag for HIM).

I told myself it was a fluke. A cosmic coincidence. A Cheesecake Factory-shaped anomaly.

Then it happened again. And again. At this point, I'm not unlucky in love—I'm a farm system. I'm developing talent for other teams.

## The Evidence Mounts

Let's review my greatest hits:

**Exhibit A:** The guy who said he "needed space to figure out what he wanted." What he wanted, it turns out, was my former spin instructor. They now have a podcast about their love story. I was not consulted for the podcast, which feels like a journalistic oversight.

**Exhibit B:** The commitment-phobe who couldn't discuss moving in together without breaking into hives. Married within a year of our breakup. To someone he met on an app. An app I recommended to *him*, by the way, back when I thought we were building a future and not, evidently, running a placement agency.

**Exhibit C:** I don't even want to talk about Exhibit C. Exhibit C got a joint Instagram account within four months. A joint account, people. I couldn't get him to consistently text back and this woman got a *branded hashtag*.

## The Theories

I've workshopped several explanations for my gift/curse/inexplicable pattern:

1. **I'm secretly a relationship whisperer**, teaching men emotional skills like empathy, communication, and how to load a dishwasher correctly, only for other women to reap the rewards. I'm basically an unpaid consultant. I should start invoicing.

2. **I have impeccable taste but terrible timing**, always arriving approximately one Personal Growth Journey too early.

3. **Men need to date me specifically to realize what they actually want**, which is apparently the opposite of me. This one stings a little, not gonna lie.

4. **It's just confirmation bias** and I'm only noticing the ones who got engaged, conveniently ignoring the exes who are still single, miserable, and definitely not thriving. (This is probably the boring, correct answer, but it's much less funny than "I am a relationship fairy godmother, minus the actual reward.")

## The Silver Lining

Look, I've made peace with it. Mostly. I've decided to reframe my "curse" as a service industry. I am the appetizer before the entrée. The opening band before the headliner. The Blockbuster before Netflix figured out what people actually wanted.

Do I sometimes lie awake wondering what it is about me that says "practice round" instead of "final answer"? Sure. Do I occasionally stalk these newly engaged women's Instagrams and think, *you're welcome*? Also yes. I'm not proud of it, but I contain multitudes.

But here's the thing: I'd rather be the woman who taught a man how to be a decent partner than the woman who just took whatever mediocre effort he was offering and called it love. I'm playing a longer game, apparently. A game where I don't win, but everyone else's love life improves dramatically.

## Silver Lining, Take Two

So if you're single and you match with one of my exes on an app, do yourself a favor: date him. Let him marinate a little longer under someone else's care, sure, but know that I did the groundwork. I planted the seeds of emotional availability. I basically did the relationship equivalent of pre-heating the oven.

You're welcome in advance.

And if *you're* one of my exes reading this (unlikely, since you're probably too busy picking out china patterns): I'm happy for you, genuinely. Just maybe send a fruit basket next time? A little acknowledgment of my role in your glow-up wouldn't kill you.

I'll be here. Single. Waiting for my magic touch to work on myself for once.

*Any day now.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a magazine-style personal narrative about heartbreak, superstition, and pattern recognition in love, including specific anecdotes like a text message breakup and losing a friend to someone else.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Astrology of Almost

I used to think I was the kind of person who didn't believe in signs. Then I got dumped over text message on a Tuesday afternoon while standing in the cereal aisle of a Trader Joe's, and suddenly I was the kind of person who noticed that the fluorescent light above me had been flickering all week.

The message itself was almost comically brief: "I don't think this is working. I think we should stop talking." No punctuation drama, no paragraph of explanation—just a period at the end like a door clicking shut. I remember reading it three times, waiting for more words to materialize, the way you refresh an email hoping the bad news will have resolved itself in the time it took to look away.

What nobody tells you about being broken up with via text is the strange archaeology it triggers. I went back through four months of messages that night, searching for the exact moment things curdled. I found it, or told myself I did: a Wednesday in March when his texts started arriving forty minutes later than usual. I built an entire mythology around those forty minutes. I decided they meant something, the way you decide a black cat crossing your path means something, the way you decide seeing 11:11 on the clock means something. It didn't. He was probably just watching television. But I needed the forty minutes to mean something because the alternative—that people simply stop loving you with no warning, no build-up, no forty-minute tell—felt unbearable.

This is the part of heartbreak nobody prepares you for: not the missing the person, but the missing of the narrative. You want there to have been a story, a discernible arc, a reason. So you become a pattern-recognition machine running on no sleep and too much wine, cross-referencing his Cancer sun with your Gemini rising, wondering if you'd just checked compatibility charts before the second date, you could have saved yourself the cereal aisle entirely.

I started reading horoscopes again for the first time since college. Not because I believed Mercury retrograde caused my phone to autocorrect "fine" to "wine" in a text to my mother, but because horoscopes offer something grief actually craves: the sense that someone, somewhere, is tracking your life with more attention than you can currently spare for yourself. When mine said "a period of releasing what no longer serves you," I wanted to laugh and cry simultaneously, because sure, fine, but nobody had asked me if I was ready to release anything.

Here's an anecdote I don't tell people right away, because it makes me sound worse than the text-message breakup makes me look sympathetic: two years before Cereal Aisle Tuesday, I lost my best friend Dana to a man named Peter.

Not lost as in death. Lost as in the slow erosion where someone you've called every single day for six years starts taking eleven hours to respond, and you tell yourself it's because she's busy, she's in love, this is normal, this is what happens—until one day you realize you haven't spoken in three weeks and the last text in the thread is you asking if she wants to get pho and her thumbs-up emoji, no words, just a thumbs-up, like you were a coworker confirming a meeting time.

Peter wasn't a villain. That's the maddening part. He didn't forbid her from seeing me or say cruel things about our friendship. He just existed, fully, completely, all-consumingly, the way new love does, and Dana poured herself into that new container until there wasn't much liquid left for the old one. I spent months doing the same archaeological digging I'd later do with the Cancer man—searching for the moment, the slight, the thing I did wrong. I decided it was a comment I'd made about Peter's job being "fine, I guess" during their second month of dating. I built a shrine to that comment. I still think about it sometimes, the same way I think about the forty minutes.

What I know now, saying it out loud in a way I couldn't admit for a long time: sometimes there is no comment, no forty minutes, no Mercury retrograde. Sometimes people's attention is a limited resource, and they spend it where the return feels highest in that particular season of their life, and you were simply not that season. This is a much harder thing to sit with than a horoscope. A horoscope tells you the universe has plans for you. The truth is often just: people's hearts are small rooms, and they can't always fit everyone who wants to live there.

But I haven't stopped checking my horoscope. I haven't stopped, if I'm honest, doing the small superstitious math of it all—counting how many times an ex's name comes up in conversation, noting when a song plays twice in one week, wondering what it means that I keep seeing the same red car. I don't actually think the universe is leaving me clues. I think I am a person, like most people, trying to make meaning out of the parts of my life that refused to give me any answers when I asked directly.

The Cancer man and I never spoke again after that text. Dana and I did, eventually—a strange, careful reunion two years later over coffee, both of us older, both of us aware of what had been lost and unable to fully name it. We didn't talk about Peter. We talked about her job, my apartment, whether either of us still liked pho as much as we used to. It was fine. It was, I guess, a beginning of something new that wasn't quite the old thing restored.

I don't think astrology predicted any of it. I don't think there was a sign in the flickering fluorescent light. But I keep looking for one anyway, the way you keep pressing on a bruise—not because you think it'll stop hurting, but because the ache, at least, feels like something you understand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an emotional first-love story in the voice of a young woman analyzing why men she likes always end up happily with someone else, ending with her decision to keep hoping anyway.
counterfactuals.output:
# Always the Almost

I've made a list. I keep making it, actually, adding to it in the margins of notebooks, in my phone at 2am, in the quiet space between songs on long drives home. It's a list of all the boys I've loved who ended up loving someone else.

Daniel, who I met at nineteen, who used to save me the last seat on the bus and call it coincidence. He's married now, to a woman who laughs loud and easy, who probably never spent a Tuesday night wondering if she was too much or not enough. I saw their engagement photos and felt something crack quietly in my chest, like ice under weight you didn't know was there.

Before him, there was Theo, who wrote me poetry disguised as text messages and then, six months later, wrote actual poetry for someone named Claire. I like to imagine I taught him how—that somewhere in his new metaphors are the ghosts of ours. It's a small, bitter comfort, claiming credit for a fire I never got to sit beside.

I used to think I was doing something wrong. I analyzed it the way you'd study a math problem you kept failing—if I could just find the error, I could fix the outcome. Maybe I loved too visibly, wore my wanting like a sign around my neck, and men don't chase what isn't hidden. Maybe I loved too quietly, and they never knew there was a fire at all, just assumed the warmth was ambient, free, not meant for them specifically.

Maybe timing. Maybe geography. Maybe I remind them of home when they're looking for someplace new.

I've cried about it in bathtubs gone cold, called my sister at midnight to ask her, half-joking, half-not, if there's something fundamentally unkeepable about me. She always says no. She always says *their loss.* I've stopped believing that phrase can hold the weight I put on it.

Here's what I know: I am the girl who gets almost. I am the almost-chosen, the nearly-loved, the one they remember fondly at weddings that aren't mine. I've built an identity out of proximity to happiness that was never quite mine to keep.

And yet.

Somewhere between the grief and the counting, I noticed something—I still slow down when I meet someone kind. I still let myself imagine, even knowing how the story tends to end. Last week a boy asked for my number and I gave it, heart stupid and hopeful, already halfway to writing his name somewhere I'd have to erase it later.

I could stop. I could build walls tall enough that almost never gets in. But I think about all those men, happy now, and instead of only grief, I feel something like proof: love is possible. It exists. It found them. Why not me, someday, with someone who stays?

So I'm keeping the list, but I'm also keeping the hope—not because I'm naive, but because the alternative is closing a door I don't actually want closed. I'd rather be the girl who almost loved and kept trying than the one who stopped believing it could ever be her turn.

Maybe next time, I won't be the almost. Maybe next time, I'll be the finally.

I'm still here, still open, still hoping.

That has to count for something.
